newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila tells Beijing to pull out Spratlys ships.
newsitem.headline: Manila tells Beijing to pull out Spratlys ships.

text.p: The Philippines has demanded China withdraw three naval ships it said had encroached on an area claimed by Manila in the Spratly Islands, and said the Chinese action could harm bilateral ties, officials said on Thursday.

The presence of the vessels in the area could also set back regional cooperation, Manila said in a diplomatic note sent to the Chinese embassy on Wednesday, acting Foreign Secretary Tomas Padilla said.
It violated a code of conduct between the two countries requiring both sides not to take any action that would disturb peace in the area, the note said.

"In order not to harm relations and set back the cooperation slowly developing in the region, the Philippine government therefore calls on the Chinese government to withdraw the three Chinese naval vessels from the vicinity of Kalayaan and Panata islands," Padilla, reading from his note, told reporters.

President Fidel Ramos ordered the filing of the protest after air force planes reported sighting the three armed ships, accompanied by fishing boats, near two of the eight islands in the Spratlys occupied by Philippine troops.
The Spratlys are a cluster of isles, reefs and shoals in the South China Sea believed to be potentially rich in oil and gas.
Beijing says the entire area historically belongs to China. The islands are also claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, Taiwan, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei.
Besides sending the note, a Department of Foreign Affairs official summoned Chinese ambasador Guan Ding-ming on Wednesday and told him of Manila's concern.
Defence Secretary Renato de Villa said on Thursday the government had received no response from Beijing.
But the Chinese embassy on Tuesday denied that China had naval ships in the area.
In addition to the three naval ships, air force planes saw several fishing boats, including a cargo-type vessel with a landing deck for helicopters, de Villa told reporters.
"We are saying that they are inside our Kalayaan municipality and that there is no prior notice, and that there has been no advice that they will be there," de Villa said.
De Villa said the vessels were first sighted on April 25 and were still in the area. New aerial photographs taken two days ago showed Chinese markings on the vessels, he said.

Tension flared between the Philippines and China in 1995 when Manila accused the Chinese of building what it said looked like naval support structures on Mischief Reef. Beijing said they were shelters for fishermen and has refused to dismantle them.
"These are armed naval ships in our categorisation because there are deck guns," de Villa said of the latest incident.
De Villa said surveillance planes also saw what appeared to be a newly-built hut-like structure near one of the Manila-claimed islands which was similar to those at Mischief Reef.
